taxonomyNote: NatureServe and the Florida Museum treat this snake as Liodytes rigida (Glossy Swampsnake), with Regina rigida as a synonym; Animal Diversity Web still files it as Regina rigida.
fieldMarks: Small, heavy-bodied snake, usually 14-24 in; glossy brown to olive-brown, sometimes with a faint dark stripe down the back and each side.
Yellow lip scales contrast sharply with the olive-brown head; lower sides yellowish-tan.
Belly yellow or cream with two rows of small black half-moon markings.
Keeled scales in 19 rows at midbody; relatively large eyes with round pupils.
behavior: Nocturnal; feeds mainly on crayfish, also small fishes, salamanders and small frogs.
Adults eat mainly crayfish; the young take small aquatic invertebrates such as dragonfly larvae.
Flees into water and dives to the bottom when approached; a captured snake may flatten its head and release musk.
Gives birth to live young (6-16) in summer; active March to early November in Texas.
habitat: Slow-moving lowland waters: cypress swamps, marshes, bogs, ponds, lakes, ditches, rice fields, streams and floodplains.
Usually secluded in crayfish or muskrat burrows, under wet vegetation or debris at the water's edge, or among aquatic plants; rarely far from water.
range: Southeastern United States, per NatureServe: Alabama, Arkansas, Florida, Georgia, Louisiana, Mississippi, North Carolina, Oklahoma, South Carolina, Texas and Virginia; in Florida from Osceola County northwest into the Panhandle.

lookalikes.name: Striped swampsnake (striped crayfish snake)
lookalikes.howToTell: Unpatterned belly and smooth body scales, versus keeled scales and a half-moon-marked belly in the glossy swampsnake (Florida Museum).

lookalikes.name: Black swampsnake
lookalikes.howToTell: Glossy black with a bright red belly (Florida Museum).
